facts.fact_text: In 2007 Mr Kasparov (the first applicant), together with other individuals representing a coalition of opposition groups, intended to take part in an anti-government rally to campaign before the forthcoming parliamentary elections.
The demonstration became known as the March of Dissenters.
The notice indicated that a meeting would be held at 12 noon on 14 April 2007 in Novopushkinskiy Park.
The notice indicated that the meeting would last until 1.30 p.m.
The notice indicated that the meeting would be followed by a march via Tverskaya Street and Okhotnyy Ryad Street to Teatralnaya Square.
The notice indicated that the march was to end at 2 p.m.
The organisers estimated that about 2,000 people would take part in the event.
According to the Government, a group of about twenty persons, including the first eight applicants, started marching down Tverskaya Street while shouting anti-government slogans on 14 April 2007.
According to the Government, the total number of people who took part in the unauthorised march on 14 April 2007 was about fifty.

Mr Kasparov (the first applicant), Mr Tarasov (the second applicant) and Mr Toropov (the fifth applicant) claimed that at 12 noon on 14 April 2007 they had been walking peacefully down Tverskaya Street towards the place of the authorised meeting at the Griboyedov monument.
The applicants did not specify the number of people walking alongside them on 14 April 2007.

On 5 April 2007 the Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government informed the organisers that the event was liable to disrupt the functioning of urban services and the movement of passers-by.

The Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government informed the organisers that authorisation could only be granted for a meeting at the foot of the Griboyedov monument on Chistoprudnyy Boulevard between 12 noon and 1.30 p.m.
The authorised meeting at the foot of the Griboyedov monument on Chistoprudnyy Boulevard was at a different location in central Moscow from the originally proposed venue.

The Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government informed the organisers that the number of participants at the authorised meeting could not exceed 1,000, the maximum capacity of the venue.
No march was authorised by the Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government.
On 10 April 2007 the Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government informed the organisers that none of the four alternative routes could be accepted.
The Department for Liaison with Security Authorities of the Moscow Government rejected the four alternative routes for the same reasons as the refusal of the original proposal.
Documents submitted by the Government reveal that on 14 April 2007 the Moscow police were reinforced by special units of the riot police (OMON).
The OMON units reinforcing the Moscow police on 14 April 2007 were brought in specially from twenty-nine regions of Russia.
The stated purpose of bringing in OMON units from twenty-nine regions of Russia on 14 April 2007 was "to protect public order and security" on that day.
According to the Government, the first eight applicants were arrested as they tried to pass from Tverskaya Street onto Red Square on 14 April 2007.
The first to eighth applicants were charged with the administrative offence of breaching the regulations on holding demonstrations.
Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) was charged with a breach of the established procedure for conducting public assemblies, an offence under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) was found to have acted in breach of the regulations on holding demonstrations and was convicted of an administrative offence under Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The second to eighth applicants were each individually convicted of having breached the procedure for the conduct of public assemblies, an administrative offence under Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

Article 20.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that breaches of the established procedure for the organisation of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets shall be punishable by an administrative fine of between ten and twenty times the minimum wage, payable by the organisers.

Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that breaches of the established procedure for the conduct of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets shall be punishable by an administrative fine of between 1,000 and 2,000 Russian roubles for the organisers, and between 500 and 1,000 Russian roubles for the participants.

Article 27.2 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the escorting or transfer by force of an individual for the purpose of drawing up an administrative offence report, if this cannot be done at the place where the offence was discovered and if the drawing-up of a report is mandatory, shall be carried out by the police.
Article 27.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the escort operation shall be carried out as quickly as possible.

Article 27.2 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the escort operation shall be recorded in an escort operation report, an administrative offence report or an administrative detention report, and that the escorted person shall be given a copy of the escort operation report if he or she so requests.

Article 27.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that administrative arrest or short-term restriction of an individual's liberty may be applied in exceptional cases if this is necessary for the prompt and proper examination of the alleged administrative offence or to secure the enforcement of any penalty imposed by a judgment concerning an administrative offence.

Article 27.3 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that where the detained person so requests, his family, the administrative department at his place of work or study and his defence counsel shall be informed of his whereabouts.

Article 27.3 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the arrested person shall have his rights and obligations under the Code explained to him, and the corresponding entry shall be made in the administrative arrest report.
Article 27.4 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the administrative arrest shall be recorded in a report.
Article 27.4 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that if he or she so requests, the arrested person shall be given a copy of the administrative arrest report.

Article 27.5 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that the duration of the administrative arrest shall not exceed three hours, except in the cases set out in paragraphs 2 and 3 of that Article.

Article 27.5 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that persons subject to administrative proceedings concerning offences involving unlawful crossing of the Russian border may be subject to administrative arrest for up to 48 hours.

Article 27.5 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provides that persons subject to administrative proceedings concerning offences punishable, among other administrative sanctions, by administrative detention may be subject to administrative arrest for up to 48 hours.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow noted the insignificant volume of the case file (five pages) and decided to hold the hearing on 14 April 2007, having postponed it first by forty-five minutes and then by an additional twenty minutes.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow rejected the motion to call eyewitnesses, holding that it was premature to call witnesses before the applicant and the police had been questioned.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District of Moscow rejected the motion to call eyewitnesses on the grounds that the persons concerned had not been mentioned in the police report and that the facts were sufficiently clear to determine the charges.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow noted that there had been no proof that the first-instance hearing had not been held in public.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow noted that there had been no proof that Mr Kasparov (the first applicant) had not been given sufficient time to prepare his defence, since he had had two hours to do so.
The applicants claimed that their way had been barred by the riot police who were blocking off several streets in central Moscow on 14 April 2007.

The applicants claimed that all pedestrians, both aspiring protesters and unsuspecting passers-by, had been pushed back, surrounded and indiscriminately beaten up by the riot police before being arrested and taken in police vans to different police stations on 14 April 2007.
Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) alleged that she had seen a policeman hitting a man with a truncheon and had intervened to try to stop the beating.
Ms Chelysheva (the ninth applicant) alleged that a policeman had kicked her on her left leg.
